problem: SNR is defined as full-scale sine power divided by noise-plus-distortion power. That is the definition of SINAD, not SNR. Standard textbooks and data sheets define SNR with harmonics excluded (noise only). ENOB is computed from SINAD, so the formula ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02 is being applied to a quantity wrongly named SNR. A student who writes this SNR definition in an exam will lose marks.
fix: Write: SNR = signal power ÷ noise power (harmonics excluded). SINAD = signal power ÷ (noise + distortion) power. Ideal SNR for a full-scale sine with ideal quantization is 6.02N + 1.76 dB. ENOB = (SINAD_measured − 1.76) / 6.02. In the text and in Q4, use SINAD_measured in the ENOB formula (data sheets often label this column SINAD or SNR+THD).

problem: "INL at that code may stay near zero because later codes add back" is wrong reasoning. INL at the missing code is fixed by the sum of DNL up to that code; later codes cannot change it. INL there is near zero only if INL just before the code was about +1.0 LSB, exactly as Q5 correctly says. The step contradicts the quiz answer.
fix: Step 6: DNL = 0 mV / 10 mV − 1 = −1 LSB, so the code is missing. INL at that code = INL(previous code) − 1 LSB. It is near zero only when INL before the code is about +1.0 LSB; otherwise the missing code shows up as a 1 LSB drop in the INL curve at that point.

problem: The same faulty reason is repeated: "INL may stay near zero because later codes add back." Later codes only affect later INL values.
fix: Say: "INL at that code falls by 1 LSB from the previous code's INL. It looks near zero only if INL before it is about +1.0 LSB; check DNL from the histogram separately."

problem: "Analog test cells at pins can force a voltage or current" overstates the standard. The test cell only switches the pin onto the analog test bus AT1/AT2; the voltage or current is forced by an external instrument connected to the bus.
fix: Write: analog test cells at pins connect the pin to the two-line analog test bus AT1/AT2, so an external instrument can force a voltage or current at the pin and measure the response.
